fixes.explanation: That's the report, friend. The Israelites settled in Goshen, "…acquired property there and became fruitful and increased greatly in number." (Genesis 47:27) Property and a growing family, all in one verse. I've had batches that rose less than that.

Not here, friend. The text says they settled in Goshen, "…acquired property there and became fruitful and increased greatly in number." (Genesis 47:27) Gaining property and growing in number is the report. You're reading a sadder verse than the one on the page.

Not in this verse, friend. The Israelites settle in Goshen, in the land of Egypt, and they acquire property there. (Genesis 47:27) The verse says they became fruitful and increased greatly in number. A trip back to Canaan isn't in it.

That's the word, friend. God told Jacob He would give the land "…to your descendants after you as an everlasting possession." (Genesis 48:4) The promise reaches to the family that comes after him. And look at that word, everlasting. That's a long time to hold a deed.

That's the spot, friend. Jacob says, "…I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath…" and the text adds, in parentheses, that Ephrath is Bethlehem. (Genesis 48:7) Jacob says Rachel died to his sorrow, so I think this memory still weighs on him.
Machpelah is a burial cave where Abraham buried Sarah (Genesis 23:19). But Jacob says he buried Rachel "…beside the road to Ephrath…" (Genesis 48:7) He names a roadside, and a cave isn't mentioned.

It's true, friend. The text says "…Israel’s eyesight was poor because of old age; he could hardly see." (Genesis 48:10) That's all the verse says about it. Keep that detail in your apron pocket, because this scene has more coming.

No officials in this one, friend. Israel says, "I never expected to see your face again, but now God has let me see your children as well." (Genesis 48:11) He's talking about Joseph's children. Joseph and his two sons are right there with him, so it's a family moment.

That's right, friend. Israel says, "…may they be called by my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth." (Genesis 48:16) He asks for his name and Abraham's and Isaac's names to be on those boys. My name is carved on a handle, and I'm proud of it, but that is a whole other level of name.

Both halves are in the blessing, friend. Israel says, "…may they be called by my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth." (Genesis 48:16) The names AND the multitude. That's a lot packed into one blessing, like a batch where every cookie got its own chocolate chips.

Not quite, friend. Joseph says, "Not so, my father! This one is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head." (Genesis 48:18) He says this one is the firstborn and asks for the right hand on his head. Nothing in his words asks for another day.

Not in this blessing, friend. Israel says, "…his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations." (Genesis 48:19) Of Manasseh he says he shall become a people and be great. Serving isn't mentioned, and nobody here gets handed an apron and a to-do list.

Sheep would be a fine gift, friend, but nobody's handing over a flock here. Israel says, "…I give the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow." (Genesis 48:22) The gift is a ridge of land. Wrap that one up if you can.
